title: Diclofenac and Alcohol: Voltaren Gel vs Tablets, Risks and Timing
excerpt: Can you drink on diclofenac? Why Voltaren gel and diclofenac tablets carry very different risks with alcohol, what happens to your stomach and kidneys, and the warning signs that need a doctor.
metaDescription: Can you drink on diclofenac? Why Voltaren gel and tablets differ with alcohol, stomach bleeding and kidney risks, timing, and warning signs to watch for.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** the form of diclofenac you're using changes the answer a lot. If you're rubbing Voltaren gel on a sore knee, only a small amount of the drug gets into your bloodstream, and an occasional drink is generally considered low concern for a healthy adult. Diclofenac tablets are a different story. Oral diclofenac is a strong NSAID (a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, the same family as ibuprofen and naproxen), and like the rest of that family it weakens your stomach's natural protection. Alcohol irritates the same lining. Together they raise the risk of ulcers and stomach bleeding, and they both put extra strain on your kidneys when you're dehydrated.

**The quick rules:** If you take diclofenac tablets, ask the doctor or pharmacist who prescribed them how much alcohol, if any, is reasonable for you. Avoid heavy or binge drinking while you're on them. Don't add Advil, Aleve, or aspirin on top of diclofenac for a hangover. If you use Voltaren gel, follow the label dose and remember that its warning still applies if you have 3 or more drinks a day. And don't take diclofenac tablets that weren't prescribed to you.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label guidance. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before drinking on diclofenac if** you take it by mouth every day, you've had a stomach ulcer or bleeding, you're 60 or older, you have heart, kidney, or liver disease, or you also take blood thinners, steroids, antidepressants such as SSRIs, or blood pressure medicines. **Get urgent medical care** for black or tarry stools, vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds, severe stomach pain, chest pain, shortness of breath, weakness on one side of the body, or slurred speech. In an emergency, call 911.

## Gel, Patch, or Tablet? Why the Form Matters So Much

Diclofenac comes in more forms than most painkillers, and they don't carry the same level of risk with alcohol. Before anything else, it helps to know which one you have.

**Topical forms (rubbed on or stuck to the skin):**

- **Voltaren Arthritis Pain gel (diclofenac sodium 1%).** Sold over the counter in the US since 2020, and widely available in other countries under the Voltaren or Voltarol name. It's meant for arthritis pain in the hands, wrists, elbows, knees, ankles, and feet.
- **Diclofenac patches** (such as Flector), usually prescribed for short-term pain from sprains and strains.
- **Diclofenac topical solution** (such as Pennsaid), a prescription liquid for knee arthritis.

**Oral forms (swallowed):**

- **Diclofenac sodium delayed-release tablets** (the original Voltaren tablets in the US, now mostly generic).
- **Diclofenac sodium extended-release tablets**, designed to release slowly through the day.
- **Diclofenac potassium tablets** (such as Cataflam), which work faster and are often used for short-term pain or menstrual cramps.
- **Diclofenac potassium powder** (Cambia), a prescription option for migraine attacks.
- **Diclofenac combined with misoprostol** (Arthrotec), where the second ingredient is added to help protect the stomach.

### Why the gel is so different

When you rub diclofenac gel into your skin, most of the drug stays in the tissue near where you applied it. Only a small fraction makes it into your blood. The prescribing information for diclofenac gel describes systemic exposure (the amount circulating through your whole body) as a small fraction of what you'd get from tablets, even at the full recommended dose. That's the whole point of a topical NSAID: you get pain relief where you need it with far less drug reaching your stomach, kidneys, and heart.

That doesn't make the gel risk-free. It's still an NSAID, and the US Drug Facts label carries the same stomach bleeding warning found on other over-the-counter NSAIDs. But in practice, the risk from an occasional drink while using the gel as directed is much lower than with tablets.

### Why the tablets need more respect

Oral diclofenac is one of the more potent NSAIDs. It's mostly prescription-only in the US, and it carries the FDA's boxed warning for all oral NSAIDs: a raised risk of serious stomach and intestinal bleeding, ulcers, and tears, and a raised risk of heart attack and stroke. Alcohol directly adds to the first of those risks and can make the others harder to manage.

If the brief version of your question is "I'm using Voltaren gel, can I have a glass of wine?", the answer for most healthy adults is that it's unlikely to be a problem. If it's "I'm on diclofenac tablets, can I go out drinking?", that's a question for your prescriber, and the general answer is to keep it light or skip it.

## How Diclofenac and Alcohol Interact: The Stomach Chemistry in Plain Words

The main risk of mixing oral diclofenac with alcohol is damage to the lining of your stomach and upper intestine. Here's why the two make each other worse.

### What diclofenac does to your stomach

Diclofenac works by blocking enzymes called COX-1 and COX-2. These enzymes make prostaglandins, chemical messengers that drive pain and swelling. Blocking them is how diclofenac eases a sore joint.

The trouble is that prostaglandins also have a protective job in your stomach. They help:

- produce the layer of mucus that coats the stomach wall,
- release bicarbonate, which neutralizes acid right at the surface,
- keep blood flowing to the lining so it can repair itself, and
- help platelets clump together to stop small bleeds.

When diclofenac lowers prostaglandins throughout your body, your stomach loses some of that protection. The acid that's always there has an easier time causing erosions and ulcers, and small bleeds are slower to stop. This is true of all oral NSAIDs, which is why they're one of the most common causes of stomach ulcers.

### What alcohol does to your stomach

Alcohol attacks the same lining from a different direction. It directly irritates the stomach wall, increases acid production, and can cause gastritis (inflammation of the stomach lining), especially in larger amounts or on an empty stomach. If you've ever had a burning stomach the morning after a big night, that's part of what's going on. Our guide to [stomach pain after drinking](/never-hungover/stomach-pain-after-drinking) explains this in more detail.

### Why the combination adds up

Put the two together and you have a stomach lining that's been weakened by diclofenac and then irritated by alcohol. That's why the US over-the-counter NSAID labels, including the label for Voltaren gel, warn that the chance of severe stomach bleeding is higher if you have 3 or more alcoholic drinks every day while using the product. The prescription labeling for oral diclofenac similarly lists alcohol use among the factors that raise the risk of stomach and intestinal bleeding, along with older age, a past ulcer, smoking, and taking other medicines that affect bleeding.

The risk isn't all-or-nothing. One drink with dinner is not the same as a night of heavy drinking. But the more you drink, and the more often, the more the risks stack.

## The Kidney Angle: Dehydration Makes NSAIDs Harder on Your Kidneys

The second concern with oral diclofenac and alcohol is your kidneys.

Prostaglandins help keep blood flowing to your kidneys, and that job matters most when you're low on fluids. Normally your kidneys rely on them to stay well supplied when you're dehydrated. NSAIDs block that backup system.

Alcohol is the other half of the problem. It suppresses a hormone called vasopressin, which normally tells your kidneys to hold on to water. With less of it, you pee more and lose fluid, which is a big reason hangovers leave you thirsty and headachy.

So the morning after heavy drinking, you can end up with a kidney that's short of fluid and a drug that has taken away its usual way of compensating. In healthy people who take a normal dose occasionally, this rarely causes harm. But the risk goes up if you:

- are older,
- already have kidney disease, heart failure, or liver disease,
- take blood pressure medicines such as ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or diuretics (water pills), or
- have been vomiting or sweating a lot and not drinking enough water.

Doctors sometimes call the combination of an NSAID, a diuretic, and an ACE inhibitor or ARB the "triple whammy" for the kidneys. Adding dehydration from alcohol to that mix is something to avoid. If you have pain in your back or side after drinking, our guide to [kidney pain after drinking](/never-hungover/kidney-pain-after-drinking) covers what it can mean and when to see a doctor.

With the gel, so little diclofenac reaches the kidneys that this is much less of a concern at the label dose, though the label still asks people with kidney problems to talk to a doctor first.

## What About the Liver?

Diclofenac's relationship with alcohol is not like Tylenol's. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) has a specific chemical interaction with alcohol in the liver, which is why its label carries a liver warning for people who drink. You can read the details in our guide to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol). Diclofenac doesn't share that mechanism.

That said, diclofenac is one of the NSAIDs more often linked to raised liver enzymes in blood tests, and rare cases of serious liver injury are described in its prescribing information. For people on long-term oral diclofenac, the labeling recommends checking liver blood tests periodically. Heavy drinking puts its own load on the liver, and the combination is a reason to tell your doctor honestly how much you drink before starting oral diclofenac, especially if you've been told you have fatty liver or other liver problems.

With the gel used as directed, liver effects are not a major concern for most people, because blood levels stay low.

## The Heart and Blood Pressure Angle

All oral NSAIDs carry a boxed warning about a raised risk of heart attack and stroke, and diclofenac is one of the NSAIDs that regulators have looked at most closely on this point. In 2013, the European Medicines Agency concluded that the heart risk with diclofenac tablets is similar to that of the newer COX-2 inhibitor drugs, and it advised against diclofenac for people with established heart disease, circulation problems, or a history of stroke.

Alcohol isn't a direct trigger for that risk the way it is for stomach bleeding. But heavy drinking raises blood pressure, NSAIDs can raise it too, and both can make the body hold on to salt and water. If you have heart disease or high blood pressure and you've been prescribed oral diclofenac, that's another reason to keep drinking modest and talk to your doctor about what's right for you.

## Other Side Effects That Alcohol Can Make Worse

Diclofenac tablets can cause dizziness and, less commonly, drowsiness. Alcohol does both. Together, they can make you less steady than you expect, which matters for driving, stairs, and anything that needs coordination. Diclofenac can also cause indigestion, nausea, and heartburn, all of which alcohol tends to make worse.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

The risk of mixing diclofenac and alcohol isn't the same for everyone. Talk to your prescriber before drinking at all if any of these apply to you:

- **You take oral diclofenac every day,** especially at higher doses or for months at a time.
- **You've had a stomach ulcer or stomach bleeding** in the past. This is one of the strongest risk factors for another one.
- **You're 60 or older.** The risk of NSAID-related stomach bleeding rises with age.
- **You take a blood thinner** (such as warfarin, apixaban, or rivaroxaban), **an antiplatelet drug** (such as clopidogrel or daily aspirin), **a steroid** (such as prednisone), **or an SSRI or SNRI antidepressant.** Each of these raises bleeding risk on its own.
- **You have kidney disease, heart failure, high blood pressure, or liver disease.**
- **You drink 3 or more drinks most days.** This is the exact threshold on the over-the-counter NSAID labels.
- **You're pregnant or trying to get pregnant.** NSAIDs are generally avoided later in pregnancy, and Arthrotec (diclofenac with misoprostol) must not be taken during pregnancy because misoprostol can cause miscarriage. Alcohol isn't advised during pregnancy either.

If none of these apply and you use diclofenac gel occasionally for joint pain, a drink now and then is unlikely to cause trouble. Your pharmacist can give you a quick, personal answer either way.

## Can You Take Diclofenac for a Hangover?

It's not a good choice, for a few reasons.

**The gel won't help.** Topical diclofenac works where you rub it in. It does nothing for a pounding head or an upset stomach, and it isn't designed to.

**Oral diclofenac is the wrong tool.** Diclofenac tablets are mostly prescription-only and are meant for arthritis, injuries, and other inflammatory pain. A hangover morning is exactly when an NSAID is hardest on you: you're often dehydrated, your stomach lining is already irritated from alcohol, and you may not have eaten. That's the worst setting for both the stomach and kidney risks described above.

**Doubling up is a real risk.** If you're already prescribed diclofenac, don't take Advil (ibuprofen), Aleve (naproxen), or aspirin on top of it to deal with a hangover. Stacking NSAIDs multiplies the stomach and kidney risks without adding much pain relief. The Voltaren gel label likewise says not to use it with other NSAIDs unless a doctor tells you to.

**Don't borrow someone else's pills.** Diclofenac tablets are prescribed with a person's age, health, and other medicines in mind. Taking someone else's prescription after a night out skips all of that.

For general hangover pain, our guide to [NSAIDs and alcohol](/never-hungover/nsaids-and-alcohol) compares the over-the-counter options and explains how to use them more safely.

## How Long Should You Wait Between Diclofenac and a Drink?

There's no official waiting time, and the answer depends on the form and how often you take it.

- **Immediate-release diclofenac** (such as diclofenac potassium) is absorbed quickly and has a short half-life in the blood, around two hours. But its effect on the stomach lining and on platelets doesn't vanish the moment blood levels fall.
- **Delayed-release and extended-release tablets** are built to keep working for many hours. If you take one in the morning, it's still active in the evening.
- **If you take diclofenac every day,** it's effectively always in your system, so there's no time of day that avoids the interaction.
- **With the gel,** you typically apply it up to four times a day, so it's also more or less continuously present, though at low blood levels.

Because of all this, trying to time a drink around your dose isn't a reliable strategy. A better approach is to keep the amount small, have it with a meal, drink water alongside it, and get your prescriber's view on what's reasonable for you.

## If You Do Drink While on Diclofenac

If your prescriber has said an occasional drink is acceptable, these habits lower the risk:

- **Take diclofenac tablets with food** as directed, and don't drink on an empty stomach. Food helps buffer the stomach. Our guide to [drinking on an empty stomach](/never-hungover/drinking-on-an-empty-stomach) explains why that matters.
- **Stick to the amount your prescriber agreed** and space drinks out. Avoid binge drinking entirely.
- **Drink water** before, during, and after alcohol to protect your kidneys.
- **Don't add other NSAIDs.** That includes ibuprofen, naproxen, aspirin, and combination cold or sinus products that contain them. Check labels.
- **Use the lowest dose for the shortest time** your prescriber recommends, which is the standard advice for all NSAIDs.
- **Watch for warning signs** like black stools, stomach pain that doesn't settle, or unusual tiredness and paleness, which can be signs of slow bleeding.

For gel users, the main rules are to stay within the label dose (the dosing card that comes with Voltaren gel tells you how much to use for each joint), not to use it for more than 21 days without talking to a doctor, and not to combine it with oral NSAIDs unless a doctor has told you to.

## Warning Signs: When to Get Help Right Away

Stomach bleeding from NSAIDs can happen without much warning, and it can be slow and quiet or sudden. Get urgent medical care if you notice:

- black, tarry, or bloody stools,
- vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds,
- severe or persistent stomach pain,
- feeling faint, dizzy, or unusually weak and pale,
- chest pain, shortness of breath, weakness on one side of the body, or slurred speech (possible heart attack or stroke),
- swelling in the legs or ankles, or peeing much less than usual (possible kidney problems), or
- yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, or pain under your right ribs (possible liver problems).

If symptoms are severe or someone is confused, collapsing, or vomiting a lot of blood, call 911.

## How Diclofenac Compares with Other Painkillers and Alcohol

If you're weighing your options, here's how diclofenac fits with the other common choices:

- **Ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin):** Shorter acting, and at over-the-counter doses it's generally considered one of the gentler NSAIDs on the stomach, but the same alcohol warning applies. See our guide to [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol).
- **Naproxen (Aleve):** Longer acting, so it stays in your system much longer after a dose. See [Aleve and alcohol](/never-hungover/aleve-and-alcohol).
- **Meloxicam (Mobic):** A once-daily prescription NSAID with a long half-life and the same stomach and kidney concerns. See [meloxicam and alcohol](/never-hungover/meloxicam-and-alcohol).
- **Aspirin:** Adds a strong, lasting effect on platelets, which makes it a particular concern for bleeding. See [aspirin and alcohol](/never-hungover/aspirin-and-alcohol).
- **Acetaminophen (Tylenol):** Not an NSAID, so it doesn't add to stomach bleeding risk, but it has its own alcohol caution for the liver.
- **Topical diclofenac gel:** For joint pain, it's one of the lowest-risk ways to use an NSAID, because so little reaches the bloodstream.

That last point is worth highlighting. For people who need regular relief from arthritis in a knee or hand and who also enjoy an occasional drink, asking a doctor whether a topical NSAID could replace or reduce oral tablets is a reasonable conversation to have.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that's studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and hangover symptoms. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with only a small amount of human data. It's promising, not proven. It does **not** protect your stomach from NSAIDs, and there's no good evidence it reduces the bleeding, kidney, or heart risks of combining diclofenac with alcohol.

If you take prescription medicines, check with your pharmacist before adding any supplement. If you want to try DHM, popular picks include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

No supplement changes the rules for diclofenac. Follow your prescription or the gel label, respect the alcohol caution, and don't stack painkillers.

## The Bottom Line

- The form matters. Voltaren gel and other topical diclofenac put only a small amount of the drug into your blood, so an occasional drink is generally low concern for a healthy adult using it as directed.
- Oral diclofenac and alcohol both weaken your stomach's defenses, and together they raise the risk of ulcers and bleeding. Alcohol use is a recognized risk factor on NSAID labels.
- Kidney strain is the second concern, especially when you're dehydrated after drinking.
- Diclofenac is one of the NSAIDs more often linked to raised liver enzymes, and oral NSAIDs carry a heart and stroke warning, so tell your doctor how much you drink.
- Timing a drink around your dose isn't reliable. Keep drinking light, have it with food and water, and ask your prescriber what's right for you.
- Don't use diclofenac for a hangover, and never add Advil, Aleve, or aspirin on top of it.
- Black stools, vomiting blood or coffee-ground material, or severe stomach pain need urgent care.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking diclofenac?**

It depends a lot on the form. With Voltaren gel or a diclofenac patch used as directed, very little of the drug reaches your bloodstream, so an occasional drink is generally considered low concern for a healthy adult. Oral diclofenac tablets are different: both the drug and alcohol weaken the stomach lining, so together they raise the risk of ulcers and bleeding. There's no official safe amount for tablets. Ask the doctor or pharmacist who prescribed it what's reasonable for you.

**Is Voltaren gel safe with alcohol?**

For most healthy adults using it at the label dose, an occasional drink while using Voltaren gel is unlikely to cause problems, because only a small share of the diclofenac is absorbed into the blood. The gel's Drug Facts label still carries the standard NSAID stomach bleeding warning, which says the risk is higher if you have 3 or more alcoholic drinks every day. If that describes you, or you've had a stomach ulcer, talk to a doctor or pharmacist before using it.

**How long after taking diclofenac can I drink?**

There's no official waiting period. Immediate-release diclofenac clears from the blood fairly quickly (its half-life is around 2 hours), but its effect on the stomach lining lasts longer, and extended-release and delayed-release tablets are designed to keep working for many hours. If you take it every day, the drug is effectively always on board. Rather than trying to time it, keep any drinking light, have it with food and water, and check with your prescriber.

**What happens if you mix diclofenac and alcohol?**

Usually nothing dramatic after one drink. The concern builds over time and with heavier drinking: both oral diclofenac and alcohol irritate and weaken the stomach lining, which raises the chance of ulcers and bleeding, and both can strain the kidneys when you're dehydrated. Some people also feel more dizzy or drowsy. Black or tarry stools, vomiting blood or coffee-ground material, or severe stomach pain need urgent medical care.

**Can I take diclofenac for a hangover?**

It isn't a good idea. Oral diclofenac is mostly a prescription drug for arthritis and injury pain, and a hangover morning, when you're often dehydrated and your stomach is already irritated, is when NSAIDs are hardest on the stomach and kidneys. Voltaren gel won't help a hangover headache at all, because it acts where you rub it in. Don't take diclofenac that wasn't prescribed to you.

**Does diclofenac affect the liver more than other NSAIDs?**

Diclofenac is one of the NSAIDs more often linked to raised liver enzymes, and its prescription labeling recommends periodic liver blood tests for people on long-term treatment. Serious liver injury is rare. Alcohol doesn't interact with diclofenac in the liver the way it does with Tylenol, but if you drink heavily or have liver disease, tell your doctor before starting oral diclofenac.

**Can I use Voltaren gel and take ibuprofen after drinking?**

The Voltaren gel label tells you not to use it with other NSAID pain relievers unless a doctor says to, because the stomach and kidney risks add up. After drinking, that matters more. If you need something by mouth for a headache, a single standard dose of acetaminophen after the alcohol has cleared and you've eaten is often the option pharmacists suggest, but it has its own liver caution, so ask a pharmacist if you're unsure.

**Does DHM make it safer to drink on diclofenac?**

There's no good evidence that DHM protects against the stomach bleeding or kidney risks of combining diclofenac with alcohol. DHM has promising research on alcohol metabolism and liver health, mostly from animal studies with limited human data. Check with your pharmacist before adding any supplement to a prescription medicine, and follow your diclofenac instructions either way.
